passage:
Dear Diary, Saturday
Last month, when I told Papa I cracked his phone screen, he shouted so the neighbours heard, and made me say "I am careless" in front of Dadi and my cousins. Everyone laughed. I cried in the bathroom.
So today, when I tore my uniform on the gate, I said a boy pushed me. Nobody pushed me. I just didn't want the shouting again. My hands shook the whole time.
Vasudha Masi found me crying on the stairs. I told her everything, even the lie. She said, "Keerthana, this is not your fault. Telling the truth should never feel this scary." Tonight she talked to Papa for a long time. He came and said sorry. I don't know yet if I believe him.

qa.q: What did Keerthana say had happened to the uniform?
qa.a: Keerthana said a boy pushed, though nobody pushed and the uniform tore on the gate.

qa.q: Why did Keerthana lie about the torn uniform?
qa.a: After being shouted at and made to say "I am careless" in front of family, Keerthana feared the same humiliation, so lying felt safer.

qa.q: What did Vasudha Masi do that helped?
qa.a: She listened to everything Keerthana told her, said it wasn't Keerthana's fault, and talked to Papa that same night.

qa.q: Why might Papa have come to say sorry after talking with Vasudha Masi?
qa.a: He may have realised that his shouting and mocking taught Keerthana that the truth was dangerous, which is why the lie happened.

grounding: A child humiliated for confessing learns that lying feels safer than the truth, until a trusted adult listens and speaks to the parent the same day.

passage:
In the village school, Vinita Ma'am had one rule for mistakes: whoever confessed stood on the bench for the whole period. One Monday morning Hafsa admitted forgetting her sums and stood there while the class giggled, ears burning.
After lunch Ma'am asked for the spelling homework. Hafsa had forgotten that too. She said, "I did it, Ma'am, but the goat ate the page." Her voice was steady. Inside she was shaking.
The new head teacher had seen Hafsa on the bench through the window that morning. That afternoon she called Hafsa in and said, "I think you were afraid of the bench. You won't be punished for the truth." Hafsa cried and told her. Before the bell, the head teacher spoke with Vinita Ma'am, and the bench rule ended that day.

qa.q: What was Vinita Ma'am's rule for mistakes?
qa.a: Whoever confessed stood on the bench for the whole period.

qa.q: Why did Hafsa lie after lunch?
qa.a: She feared being humiliated on the bench again while the class giggled, so a lie felt safer than confessing.

qa.q: What did the head teacher do that helped?
qa.a: She called Hafsa in calmly, named the fear, promised no punishment for the truth, and spoke to Vinita Ma'am the same day to end the rule.

qa.q: How might the other children change after the bench rule ends?
qa.a: They may feel safer admitting mistakes, instead of learning, like Hafsa, that lying is safer than the truth.

grounding: A girl humiliated for confessing at school learns to lie, showing that fear of punishment teaches deception until an adult makes the truth safe.
